profile.surgeries: Born at 36 weeks; Three urinary tract infections with fever before age 3 (two emergency visits); A kidney ultrasound was recommended in 2022 but never done after we moved
profile.family_other: Paternal grandfather: kidney problems (on dialysis in his 60s); Mother: migraines
profile.main_concern:
Theo has had headaches most mornings for two weeks, he's always thirsty and he has started wetting the bed again. Urgent care said his labs were fine, but he's one of the shortest in his class now and he isn't himself.

Symptoms: Morning headaches (about 3 weeks): Forehead; sometimes better after breakfast.; Very thirsty, drinking a lot of water (about 2 months); Waking at night to urinate; bedwetting again (about 1 month): Had been dry at night since age 4.; Tired, less active (about 2 months); Poor appetite (about 2 months); Seems shorter than classmates (this school year): Shoe and clothing sizes barely changed in a year.

My questions: Urgent care said his labs were normal. Are they normal for a 7-year-old? Why is he so thirsty and wetting the bed? Should we be worried about his growth?

summary.plain_language_summary: Theo’s symptoms and test results deserve prompt review by his pediatrician, using standards for a 7-year-old rather than adult lab ranges. The recorded blood pressure is concerningly high for his age, especially with recurring morning headaches, and should be checked again urgently today. The creatinine result, estimated kidney-function calculation, and urine protein result also need confirmation and interpretation by his care team. His marked slowing in height gain and downward shift in height percentile should be reviewed alongside the thirst, nighttime urination, and renewed bedwetting. His glucose was 92 mg/dL, but that single result does not explain these ongoing symptoms. The low hemoglobin and hematocrit, together with the recorded pallor and tiredness, are worth discussing; whether they are related needs clinical assessment. The phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase flags may reflect adult reference ranges and need age-appropriate interpretation.

key_findings.text: A blood pressure of 122/80 was reported as concerningly high for a 7-year-old, and recurring morning headaches are also reported.
Creatinine was 0.98 mg/dL, above the approximate school-age range cited by nephrology; the calculated bedside Schwartz estimate was about 49 mL/min/1.73 m² and needs clinical confirmation.
The urine dipstick showed 1+ protein in a dilute sample. A single dipstick result does not establish whether protein is persistent.
Theo has persistent thirst, nighttime urination, and renewed bedwetting; the reported glucose of 92 mg/dL is within the usual range for a child but does not explain these symptoms.
His recorded height percentile fell from about the 57th to the 6th, with about 2 cm of height gain over the year compared with the record's typical 5–6 cm at this age.
Hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL and hematocrit 33.1% were described as mildly low using approximate pediatric ranges; the urgent-care note also records pallor and reduced energy.
The phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase flags were based on adult ranges and need interpretation using age-appropriate ranges; they may be normal for a growing child.
The urgent-care note records a normal neurologic exam and no neck stiffness, but these findings do not explain the ongoing symptoms.

connections.text: The high blood pressure reading and recurring morning headaches occur together, so ask the pediatrician to review them together and arrange prompt repeat blood-pressure measurement.

Thirst, nighttime urination, renewed bedwetting, and dilute urine occur alongside the elevated creatinine estimate and positive urine protein screen; the team can consider these findings together rather than separately.

The slowed height gain and downward shift in height percentile occur alongside the urinary symptoms and kidney screening findings, making a combined review of growth and kidney-related results worth asking about.
Pallor and reduced energy occur with mildly low hemoglobin and hematocrit; ask whether these blood-count findings need follow-up while also assessing the broader symptoms.
Reported regular ibuprofen use is worth reviewing alongside the kidney screening results; those results do not by themselves establish kidney disease.

SYNTHETIC TEST DOCUMENT - FICTIONAL PATIENT - NOT REAL MEDICAL DATA

NORTHSIDE URGENT CARE - VISIT NOTE
Patient: Theo Lindqvist    DOB: 04/02/2019 (7 y)    Visit: 09/20/2026
Clinician: Jordan Kim, PA-C
Accompanied by: father (Erik Lindqvist)

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Headaches for 2 weeks; tired.

HISTORY (per father)
Frontal headaches most mornings for 2 weeks. More tired than usual, less
interested in playing. Drinking a lot of water, waking at night to pass
urine, and two recent bedwetting episodes after being dry for years.
Eating less. No vomiting, no fever, no vision changes, no head injury.

VITAL SIGNS
Temp 36.9 C   HR 92   BP 122/80   RR 20   SpO2 99%
Weight 20.1 kg   Height 116 cm

EXAM
Well appearing, somewhat pale. Neurologic exam normal; no neck stiffness.
Throat and ears normal. Heart and lungs normal.

LABS: Drawn today, see lab report. Alkaline phosphatase and phosphorus
flagged high by the lab; likely normal for a growing child. Hemoglobin
mildly low; suggested iron-rich foods. Kidney function within normal
limits. Urine dilute.

ASSESSMENT
Headache, likely tension-type or viral. Blood pressure within normal
limits.

PLAN
Ibuprofen 200 mg by mouth every 6-8 hours as needed for headache.
Encourage fluids. Follow up with pediatrician if not improved in 1 week.
